lessons.title: Measures of Center and Distribution Shapes
lessons.description: Calculate and interpret mean, median, and mode, and understand how distribution shape affects which measure is best!
lessons.formula:
Mean = sum of all values / number of values
Median = middle value when sorted
Mode = most frequent value

Symmetric: mean = median = mode
Right-skewed: mean > median > mode
Left-skewed: mean < median < mode
lessons.content:
Measures of center summarize a data set with a single typical value. The mean (average) uses every data point: add them all and divide by the count. The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the most frequent value. Each has different strengths depending on the data distribution.

The shape of the distribution determines which measure is most appropriate. In a symmetric distribution (like a bell curve), all three measures are approximately equal. In a right-skewed distribution (long tail to the right, like income data), the mean is pulled higher than the median by extreme values. In a left-skewed distribution, the mean is pulled lower.

When outliers are present, the median is usually more representative than the mean. For example, if nine people earn $40,000 and one earns $1,000,000, the mean is $136,000 but the median is $40,000. The median better represents the 'typical' person. Always consider the distribution shape when choosing your measure of center!
steps: Sort the data from smallest to largest
Calculate the mean: sum all values and divide by count
Find the median: middle value (or average of two middle values)
Identify the mode: most frequent value
Determine the shape: symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed

examples.title: Choosing the Right Measure
examples.text: Home prices in a neighborhood: $200K, $210K, $195K, $205K, $2,000,000. Mean=$562K (misleading), Median=$205K (representative). Use median for skewed data!

examples.title: Mode for Categorical Data
examples.text: Favorite colors: Red, Blue, Blue, Green, Blue, Red. Mean and median do not work for categories! Mode = Blue (appears 3 times).

lessons.tip: Remember: Mean is pulled toward the tail in skewed data. 'Mean is mean to outliers!' The median resists outliers and is usually the better measure for real-world data.

quiz.q: Data: 3, 5, 5, 7, 9. Mean?
quiz.explanation: Sum = 29, count = 5. Mean = 29/5 = 5.8.

quiz.q: For right-skewed data, which is largest?
quiz.explanation: Right-skewed: tail pulls mean right (higher). Mean > Median > Mode.

quiz.q: Best measure for income data:
quiz.explanation: Income is right-skewed with outliers. Median is most representative.
4 appears most frequently (3 times). Mode = 4.

lessons.title: Standard Deviation and the Normal Distribution
lessons.description: Calculate standard deviation, interpret the 68-95-99.7 rule, and use z-scores!
lessons.formula:
Standard Deviation:
sigma = sqrt( sum((x - mean)^2) / N )

68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD

Z-score: z = (x - mean) / sigma
lessons.content:
Standard deviation measures how spread out data is from the mean. A small SD means data clusters tightly around the mean; a large SD means data is widely scattered. First find the variance (average of squared deviations from mean), then take the square root to get standard deviation.

In a normal distribution (bell curve), the mean, median, and mode are all equal, and the data follows the 68-95-99.7 rule. This means 68% of values fall within one SD of the mean, 95% within two SDs, and 99.7% within three SDs. This rule lets you quickly estimate probabilities and proportions.

A z-score converts any value to the number of standard deviations it is from the mean. A z-score of 1.5 means the value is 1.5 SDs above average. Z-scores standardize different distributions so they can be compared directly. SAT score of 700 (mean 500, SD 100) has z=2, meaning it is 2 SD above average.
steps: Calculate the mean of the data
Find each deviation: x - mean
Square each deviation
Find the average of squared deviations (variance)
Take the square root: SD = sqrt(variance)

examples.title: Using Z-Scores
examples.text: Test score 85, class mean 72, SD 6.5. z = (85-72)/6.5 = 2.0. This student scored 2 standard deviations above the class average!

lessons.tip: The SD is in the SAME UNITS as the original data. If heights are in inches, SD is in inches. If test scores are points, SD is in points. This makes SD intuitive and interpretable!

quiz.q: Data: 10, 10, 10, 10. Standard deviation?
quiz.explanation: All values equal the mean. No deviation. SD = 0.

quiz.q: Mean=100, SD=15. What range has 68% of data?
A z-score of -1.5 means:
quiz.explanation: Negative z-score = below the mean. 1.5 SDs below.

lessons.title: The Normal Distribution and Calculating Z-Scores
lessons.description: Calculate and interpret z-scores to standardize data and find probabilities under the normal curve.
lessons.formula:
Z-Score Formula:
  z = (x − μ) / σ

Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7):
  68% of data falls within μ ± 1σ
  95% of data falls within μ ± 2σ
  99.7% of data falls within μ ± 3σ

Standard Normal Distribution:
  Mean (μ) = 0, Standard Deviation (σ) = 1

Probability between two z-values:
  P(a < Z < b) = P(Z < b) − P(Z < a)
lessons.content:
The normal distribution is the most important probability distribution in statistics. Its bell-shaped curve is symmetric about the mean, with the highest probability density at the center and probabilities tapering off equally in both directions. Many natural phenomena — heights, test scores, measurement errors — approximate a normal distribution. A normal distribution is fully described by two parameters: the mean (μ), which locates the center, and the standard deviation (σ), which controls the spread.

A z-score measures how many standard deviations a particular value is from the mean. The formula z = (x − μ) / σ converts any normal distribution to the standard normal distribution (mean = 0, std = 1). A positive z-score means the value is above average; a negative z-score means it is below average. Z-scores allow you to compare scores from different distributions and find probabilities using the standard normal table (z-table).

The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7) provides quick estimates: approximately 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three. For precise probabilities, use the z-table or a calculator to find the area under the curve. Percentiles tell you what percentage of data falls below a given value, and converting between z-scores and percentiles is a fundamental skill in statistical analysis.
steps: Identify the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of the distribution.
Calculate the z-score using z = (x − μ) / σ for the value of interest.
Use the standard normal table (z-table) or calculator to find the cumulative probability P(Z < z) for the computed z-score.
For a range of values, find P(Z < b) − P(Z < a), or use the Empirical Rule for quick estimates when z-values are near 1, 2, or 3.
Interpret the result in context: convert the probability to a percentage, find the percentile, and relate it back to the original units of the data.

examples.title: Calculating a Z-Score
examples.text: A college entrance exam has μ = 500 and σ = 100. If a student scores 650, what is their z-score? z = (650 − 500) / 100 = 150 / 100 = 1.5. This means the student scored 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. Using the z-table, P(Z < 1.5) ≈ 0.9332, so the student scored higher than about 93.3% of test-takers — roughly the 93rd percentile.

examples.title: Finding a Percentile
examples.text: The heights of adult women are normally distributed with μ = 65 inches and σ = 2.5 inches. What percentile is a woman who is 70 inches tall? z = (70 − 65) / 2.5 = 5 / 2.5 = 2.0. From the z-table, P(Z < 2.0) ≈ 0.9772. So a woman who is 70 inches tall is at approximately the 97.7th percentile — taller than about 97.7% of adult women.

lessons.tip: When the z-score is negative, the value is below the mean. A z-score of −1.5 means 1.5 standard deviations below average — always include the sign when interpreting results!

quiz.q: A z-score of 0 means the value is:
quiz.explanation: A z-score of 0 means x = μ, so the value equals the mean.

quiz.q: According to the Empirical Rule, approximately what percentage of data falls within μ ± 2σ?
quiz.explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule states that about 95% of data falls within two standard deviations of the mean.

quiz.q: If μ = 100 and σ = 15, the z-score for x = 130 is:
A z-score of −1.96 corresponds approximately to which percentile?
quiz.explanation: P(Z < −1.96) ≈ 0.025, which is the 2.5th percentile.

lessons.title: Confidence Intervals and Margin of Error
lessons.description: Construct and interpret confidence intervals for population parameters!
lessons.formula:
Confidence Interval:
Point Estimate +/- Margin of Error

Margin of Error = z* x (SD / sqrt(n))
z* = 1.96 for 95% confidence

95% CI: x-bar +/- 1.96 x (s / sqrt(n))
lessons.content:
A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on sample data. Instead of saying 'the average is 50,' we say 'we are 95% confident the average is between 47 and 53.' The interval has two parts: the point estimate (the sample statistic) and the margin of error (how far we allow for uncertainty).

The confidence level (usually 95%) means: if we repeated the sampling process many times, 95% of our intervals would contain the true population parameter. It does NOT mean there is a 95% chance the true value is in this specific interval. The true value either is or is not in the interval.

Margin of error depends on three factors: the confidence level (higher confidence = wider interval), the sample size (larger sample = smaller margin), and the data variability (more variable data = wider interval). Doubling the sample size does NOT halve the margin because of the square root in the formula. To halve the margin, you need 4 times the sample size!
steps: Find the sample statistic (mean, proportion, etc.)
Determine the confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%)
Find the critical z-value (1.645, 1.96, or 2.576)
Calculate margin of error: z* x (SD/sqrt(n))
Construct the interval: statistic +/- margin

examples.title: Effect of Sample Size
examples.text: Same data with n=400: MOE = 1.96 x (8/20) = 0.784. Quadrupling n halved the MOE! CI: (71.22, 72.78).

lessons.tip: When you see a poll result like '52% +/- 3%', the 52% is the point estimate and 3% is the margin of error. The confidence interval is 49% to 55%. The confidence level is usually 95% unless stated!

quiz.q: Sample mean=50, MOE=3. What is the 95% CI?
To halve the margin of error, you need:
quiz.explanation: MOE involves 1/sqrt(n). To halve: 1/sqrt(4n) = (1/2)(1/sqrt(n)). Need 4x n.

quiz.q: What does 95% confidence mean?
options: 95% chance true value is in interval
95% of such intervals contain true value
quiz.explanation: 95% of intervals constructed this way contain the true parameter.

quiz.q: Higher confidence level means:
quiz.explanation: More confidence = larger critical z-value = wider interval.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing and P-Values
lessons.description: Formulate hypotheses, calculate test statistics, find p-values, and make decisions!
lessons.formula:
H0: null hypothesis (status quo)
Ha: alternative hypothesis (claim to test)

Test statistic: z = (x-bar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))

Decision: if p-value < alpha, reject H0
Common alpha levels: 0.05 and 0.01
lessons.content:
Hypothesis testing is the scientific method of statistics. You start with a null hypothesis (H0) that represents the status quo or no effect, and an alternative hypothesis (Ha) that represents what you are trying to prove. You collect sample data and calculate a test statistic to determine whether the data provides enough evidence to reject H0.

The p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as yours, assuming H0 is true. A small p-value (typically less than 0.05) means the data is unlikely under H0, so you reject the null hypothesis. A large p-value means the data is consistent with H0, so you fail to reject it. 'Fail to reject' does NOT mean H0 is true!

Two types of errors can occur. A Type I error (false positive) is rejecting H0 when it is actually true (like convicting an innocent person). A Type II error (false negative) is failing to reject H0 when it is actually false (like letting a guilty person go free). The significance level alpha controls the Type I error rate.
steps: State H0 and Ha clearly
Choose alpha (significance level), usually 0.05
Calculate the test statistic from sample data
Find the p-value (probability of result assuming H0)
Compare p-value to alpha: if p < alpha, reject H0

examples.title: Testing a Mean
examples.text: H0: mean=100, Ha: mean>100. Sample: n=36, x-bar=105, SD=12. z=(105-100)/(12/6)=2.5. p-value=0.006. Since 0.006 < 0.05, reject H0. Evidence suggests mean > 100.

examples.title: Understanding Errors
examples.text: A drug is actually ineffective (H0 true). If our test rejects H0, we made a Type I error (false positive). We incorrectly concluded the drug works.

lessons.tip: Think of hypothesis testing like a court trial. H0 = 'innocent until proven guilty.' Ha = 'guilty.' The prosecution must provide evidence 'beyond a reasonable doubt' (p < alpha) to convict (reject H0).

quiz.q: p-value = 0.03, alpha = 0.05. Decision?
quiz.explanation: 0.03 < 0.05. Reject the null hypothesis.

quiz.q: A Type I error is:
quiz.explanation: Type I = false positive: rejecting H0 when it is true.

quiz.q: p-value = 0.15, alpha = 0.05. Decision?
quiz.explanation: 0.15 > 0.05. Not enough evidence to reject.

quiz.q: H0: mu=50, Ha: mu not equal 50. This is:
quiz.explanation: 'not equal to' means differences in both directions matter.

lessons.title: The Central Limit Theorem
lessons.description: Understand why the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal regardless of population shape.
lessons.formula:
Central Limit Theorem (CLT):
For large n (n ≥ 30), the sampling distribution
of the sample mean X̄ is approximately normal:

  X̄ ~ N(μ, σ/√n)

  Mean of X̄ = μ (same as population mean)
  Standard Error = σ / √n

As n increases, the sampling distribution
of X̄ approaches a normal distribution,
regardless of the shape of the population.
lessons.content:
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) is one of the most remarkable results in all of statistics. It states that regardless of the shape of the population distribution — whether it is uniform, skewed, bimodal, or any other shape — the sampling distribution of the sample mean will be approximately normal as long as the sample size is sufficiently large (typically n ≥ 30). This is why the normal distribution appears so frequently in statistical inference, even when the underlying data is not normally distributed.

Here is why this matters in practice: when you take many random samples of size n from a population and compute the mean of each sample, those means form their own distribution — the sampling distribution of X̄. The CLT tells us three things about this distribution: (1) its mean equals the population mean μ, (2) its standard deviation (called the standard error) equals σ/√n, which shrinks as the sample size grows, and (3) its shape approaches normal for large n. A larger sample size produces a tighter, more peaked sampling distribution centered on μ.

The practical consequence is enormous: the CLT justifies the use of normal-distribution-based methods for constructing confidence intervals and performing hypothesis tests about population means, even when the population itself is not normally distributed. For example, if you survey 50 randomly selected customers about their spending, the average spending from your sample will be approximately normally distributed around the true population average, regardless of how spending is distributed among all customers.
steps: Identify the population parameters: population mean μ and population standard deviation σ.
Determine the sample size n and verify that it is large enough (n ≥ 30 for the CLT to apply; smaller if the population is known to be normal).
Calculate the standard error: SE = σ / √n, which measures the typical distance between X̄ and μ.
Use the normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation SE to find probabilities, confidence intervals, or critical values for the sample mean.
Interpret results in context: larger samples give smaller standard errors and more precise estimates of the population mean.

examples.title: Dice Rolling Simulation
examples.text: Roll a single fair die: outcomes 1–6 are uniformly distributed (flat), clearly not normal. But roll the die 50 times and take the average of those 50 rolls. Repeat this many times. The CLT guarantees that the distribution of these sample means will be approximately normal with mean = 3.5 and standard error = 1.71/√50 ≈ 0.242. Even though each roll is uniform, the average of 50 rolls is nearly bell-shaped!

examples.title: Real-World Example: Household Income
examples.text: Household income in a city is right-skewed (not normal), with μ = $65,000 and σ = $20,000. An economist surveys 100 randomly selected households. By the CLT, the sample mean income X̄ is approximately normal with mean = $65,000 and SE = $20,000/√100 = $2,000. The probability that the sample average is between $63,000 and $67,000 is P(−1 < Z < 1) ≈ 0.6827, or about 68%. This works even though individual incomes are heavily skewed!

lessons.tip: The CLT works magic: any population shape becomes normal in the sampling distribution when n is large enough. If the population is already normal, the CLT holds for any sample size, even n = 1!

quiz.q: The Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal when:
options: The sample size is at least 30
quiz.explanation: For n ≥ 30, the CLT guarantees the sampling distribution of X̄ is approximately normal regardless of the population shape.

quiz.q: The standard error of the mean is calculated as:
quiz.explanation: The standard error (SE) equals σ/√n, the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.

quiz.q: As the sample size increases, the standard error:
quiz.explanation: SE = σ/√n decreases as n increases, meaning larger samples give more precise estimates.

quiz.q: A population has μ = 50 and σ = 10. For n = 100, the sampling distribution of X̄ has:
quiz.explanation: Mean of X̄ = μ = 50, and SE = 10/√100 = 1.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing Foundations
lessons.description: Formulate null and alternative hypotheses, calculate test statistics, and make decisions using p-values.
lessons.formula:
Hypotheses:
  H₀: μ = μ₀  (null hypothesis)
  H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ (two-tailed)
     μ > μ₀ (right-tailed)
     μ < μ₀ (left-tailed)

Test Statistics:
  z = (X̄ − μ₀) / (σ/√n)    [known σ]
  t = (X̄ − μ₀) / (s/√n)    [unknown σ]

Decision Rule:
  p-value < α  →  Reject H₀
  p-value ≥ α  →  Fail to reject H₀

Significance level: α = 0.05 (most common)

Type I Error: Rejecting H₀ when it is true (false positive)
Type II Error: Failing to reject H₀ when it is false (false negative)
lessons.content:
Hypothesis testing is the backbone of statistical inference. It provides a formal, objective framework for making decisions about population parameters based on sample data. The process begins by stating two competing claims: the null hypothesis (H₀), which represents the status quo or a baseline assumption (typically that there is no effect or no difference), and the alternative hypothesis (H₁), which represents what you are trying to provide evidence for. The goal is to determine whether the sample data provides sufficient evidence against H₀ in favor of H₁.

The test statistic measures how far the sample statistic is from the null hypothesis value in standard error units. For testing a population mean with known standard deviation, you use the z-statistic z = (X̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n); when σ is unknown and estimated by the sample standard deviation s, you use the t-statistic instead. The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one computed, assuming H₀ is true. A small p-value indicates that the observed data would be unlikely if H₀ were true, providing evidence against the null. If the p-value is less than the predetermined significance level α (commonly 0.05), you reject H₀.

Two types of errors can occur: a Type I error (false positive) happens when you reject a true null hypothesis, and a Type II error (false negative) occurs when you fail to reject a false null hypothesis. The significance level α is the probability of a Type I error. Tests can be one-tailed (testing for an effect in a specific direction) or two-tailed (testing for any difference), with two-tailed tests generally being more conservative. Understanding these concepts is essential for designing experiments, interpreting research findings, and making data-driven decisions in science, medicine, business, and public policy.
steps: State the null hypothesis H₀ and the alternative hypothesis H₁. Decide whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed.
Choose the significance level α (commonly 0.05) and identify the appropriate test statistic (z or t) based on whether the population standard deviation is known.
Calculate the test statistic using the sample data: z = (X̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n) or t = (X̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n).
Find the p-value: the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one calculated, assuming H₀ is true. For two-tailed tests, double the one-tailed p-value.

Make a decision: if p-value < α, reject H₀ and conclude there is statistically significant evidence for H₁. If p-value ≥ α, fail to reject H₀ — the data does not provide sufficient evidence against the null.

examples.title: Testing Whether a Mean Differs from a Claim
examples.text:
A bakery claims their bagels weigh an average of 120g. A quality inspector randomly samples 36 bagels and finds X̄ = 115g with s = 12g. Test H₀: μ = 120 vs H₁: μ ≠ 120 at α = 0.05.

Since σ is unknown, use t = (115 − 120)/(12/√36) = −5/2 = −2.5 with df = 35. The p-value for t = −2.5 (two-tailed) is approximately 0.017, which is less than 0.05. Reject H₀: there is significant evidence that the true average bagel weight differs from 120g.

examples.title: One-Tailed Test: Is the Average Greater Than Claimed?
examples.text:
A fitness center claims its members lose an average of 5 lbs in the first month. A researcher samples 25 members and finds X̄ = 6.2 lbs with s = 2.8 lbs. Test H₀: μ = 5 vs H₁: μ > 5 at α = 0.05.

t = (6.2 − 5)/(2.8/√25) = 1.2/0.56 = 2.14 with df = 24. The one-tailed p-value is approximately 0.022, which is less than 0.05. Reject H₀: there is significant evidence that the average weight loss is greater than 5 lbs in the first month.

lessons.tip: Always write your hypotheses BEFORE looking at the data. Your hypotheses should be driven by the research question, not by the results. This prevents bias and ensures the integrity of the test.

quiz.q: The null hypothesis (H₀) always represents:
options: What the researcher hopes to prove
The status quo or no effect
quiz.explanation: H₀ represents the default assumption — typically that there is no effect, no difference, or that a parameter equals a specific value.

quiz.q: If the p-value is 0.03 and α = 0.05, you should:
quiz.explanation: Since 0.03 < 0.05, the p-value is less than α, so we reject the null hypothesis.

quiz.q: A Type I error occurs when:
options: You fail to reject a false H₀
quiz.explanation: A Type I error (false positive) means rejecting H₀ when it is actually true. The probability of this error equals α.

quiz.q: For a two-tailed test with α = 0.05, the rejection regions are:
quiz.explanation: In a two-tailed test, α is split equally between both tails: 0.025 in the left tail and 0.025 in the right tail.

lessons.title: The Student's t-Test
lessons.description: Use the t-distribution to test hypotheses about population means when the population standard deviation is unknown.
lessons.formula:
t = (X̄ - μ₀) / (s / √n)

Where:
  X̄ = sample mean
  μ₀ = hypothesized population mean
  s = sample standard deviation
  n = sample size

Degrees of freedom: df = n - 1
Compare t-statistic to critical t-value from t-distribution table.
lessons.content:
The Student's t-test is a statistical method for testing whether a sample mean significantly differs from a hypothesized population mean. You use it instead of a z-test when the population standard deviation (σ) is unknown — which is almost always the case in real research. Instead of σ, you use the sample standard deviation (s), and the resulting test statistic follows a t-distribution rather than a normal distribution. The t-distribution looks like a normal bell curve but has heavier tails, meaning it accounts for the extra uncertainty when estimating σ from a small sample.

The t-distribution's shape depends on its degrees of freedom (df), calculated as n − 1 for a one-sample t-test. With a large sample (say n > 30), the t-distribution is nearly identical to the normal distribution. But with small samples, the heavier tails mean you need a larger t-value to achieve statistical significance, making the test more conservative. To perform the test: calculate your t-statistic using t = (X̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n), then compare it to the critical t-value from a t-table using your chosen significance level (usually α = 0.05) and degrees of freedom. If |t| exceeds the critical value, you reject the null hypothesis.

There are three main types of t-tests: a one-sample t-test compares one sample mean to a known value; a two-sample (independent) t-test compares means from two separate groups; and a paired t-test compares means from the same group at different times (like before and after a treatment). Each type has a slightly different formula and df calculation, but they all rely on the t-distribution. Reading a t-table: find your df in the left column, then read across to your significance level to find the critical value.
steps: State the null hypothesis (H₀) and alternative hypothesis (H₁)
Calculate the t-statistic: t = (X̄ - μ₀) / (s / √n)
Determine degrees of freedom: df = n - 1
Find the critical t-value from a t-distribution table using df and significance level α
Compare your t-statistic to the critical value: if |t| > critical value, reject H₀

examples.title: One-Sample t-Test Example
examples.text: A coffee shop claims their medium cups contain 16 oz. A sample of 10 cups has mean X̄ = 15.4 oz and s = 0.8 oz. t = (15.4 - 16) / (0.8 / √10) = -0.6 / 0.253 = -2.37. With df = 9 and α = 0.05, critical value ≈ ±2.262. Since |-2.37| > 2.262, reject H₀ — the cups contain less than 16 oz.

examples.title: Large Sample t-Test
examples.text: A school claims average test score is 75. A sample of 36 students has X̄ = 78 and s = 12. t = (78 - 75) / (12 / √36) = 3 / 2 = 1.5. df = 35, critical value ≈ ±2.030. Since |1.5| < 2.030, fail to reject H₀ — no significant evidence the average differs from 75.

lessons.tip: Use a t-test instead of a z-test whenever you're using the sample standard deviation (s) instead of the population standard deviation (σ). With large samples (n > 30), t and z give very similar results, but the t-test is technically always correct when σ is unknown.

quiz.q: When should you use a t-test instead of a z-test?
options: When the sample size is over 100
When the population standard deviation is unknown
When the population mean is known
quiz.explanation: Use a t-test when the population standard deviation (σ) is unknown and must be estimated from the sample standard deviation (s).

quiz.q: What are the degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-test with n = 20?
quiz.explanation: For a one-sample t-test, df = n - 1 = 20 - 1 = 19.

quiz.q: How does the t-distribution compare to the normal distribution?
quiz.explanation: The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution, meaning more probability is in the extremes. As df increases, it approaches the normal distribution.

quiz.q: If your calculated t-statistic is -2.5 and the critical value is ±2.145, what decision do you make?
quiz.explanation: Since |-2.5| = 2.5 > 2.145 (the critical value), the result is statistically significant. Reject the null hypothesis H₀.

lessons.title: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Theorem
lessons.description: Calculate probability given prior information using conditional probability and Bayes' formula!
lessons.formula:
Conditional Probability:
P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

Bayes' Theorem:
P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B)

Independence: P(A|B) = P(A)
lessons.content:
Conditional probability calculates the probability of an event GIVEN that another event has already occurred. Written P(A|B), it reads 'the probability of A given B.' For example, the probability of drawing a heart from a deck is 13/52 = 1/4. But if you know the card is red, the conditional probability of a heart becomes 13/26 = 1/2.

Bayes' theorem reverses conditional probability: it lets you find P(A|B) when you know P(B|A). This is incredibly powerful for medical testing, spam filtering, and detective work. If a disease affects 1% of people and a test is 99% accurate, Bayes' theorem reveals that a positive result only means about 50% chance of actually having the disease (due to the low prior probability).

Events A and B are independent if knowing B does not change the probability of A: P(A|B) = P(A). For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Flipping a fair coin and rolling a die are independent events. Drawing cards without replacement are dependent events.
steps: Identify what you know and what you need to find
For P(A|B): find P(A and B) and P(B)
Use a two-way table or tree diagram to organize information
For Bayes': identify P(B|A), P(A), and P(B)
Apply the formula and interpret the result in context

examples.title: Medical Test Example
examples.text: Disease prevalence 1%, test 99% accurate. P(disease|positive) = P(pos|dis)xP(dis)/P(pos) = 0.99x0.01 / (0.99x0.01 + 0.01x0.99) = 0.5. Only 50% chance despite 99% accurate test!

examples.title: Two-Way Table
examples.text: 100 students: 60 like math, 40 like science, 20 like both. P(math|science) = 20/40 = 0.5. P(both) = 20/100 = 0.2.

lessons.tip: Bayes' theorem is counterintuitive! Always check: is the prior probability (base rate) low? If so, even a very accurate test can give misleading positive results. This is called the 'base rate fallacy.'

quiz.q: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). If P(A and B)=0.2 and P(B)=0.5, P(A|B)=?
If P(A|B) = P(A), then A and B are:
quiz.explanation: Knowing B does not change A's probability. They are independent.

quiz.q: A bag has 5 red, 3 blue marbles. After removing one red, P(blue)?
quiz.explanation: Now 3 blue out of 7 total. P = 3/7.

quiz.q: Bayes' theorem is used to:
quiz.explanation: Bayes' theorem reverses the condition: find P(A|B) when you know P(B|A).

lessons.title: Correlation and Linear Regression
lessons.description: Calculate correlation, create best-fit lines, and understand that correlation does not imply causation!
lessons.formula:
Correlation: r = -1 to +1
r > 0: positive association
r < 0: negative association
|r| near 1: strong, near 0: weak

Regression line: y = mx + b
m = r x (Sy/Sx)
b = y-bar - m x x-bar
lessons.content:
Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables. The correlation coefficient r ranges from -1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive), with 0 meaning no linear relationship. Correlation of 0.87 indicates a strong positive association; -0.32 indicates a weak negative association.

A scatter plot displays paired data as points, letting you visually assess the relationship. The line of best fit (regression line) minimizes the total squared distances between the data points and the line (least squares method). This line can be used for prediction, but only within the range of the data.

The golden rule of statistics: correlation does NOT imply causation! Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are positively correlated, but eating ice cream does not cause drowning. Both increase during summer due to a lurking variable (temperature). Always consider whether a confounding variable might explain the observed relationship.
steps: Create a scatter plot of the paired data
Calculate the correlation coefficient r
Assess strength: |r| near 1 = strong, near 0 = weak
Assess direction: r > 0 = positive, r < 0 = negative
Find the regression line for prediction: y = mx + b

examples.title: Interpreting Correlation
examples.text: Study hours vs test scores: r = 0.85. Strong positive correlation — more studying is associated with higher scores. But does studying CAUSE scores? Not necessarily (ability could be a confounder).

examples.title: Prediction with Regression
examples.text: Regression line: score = 5.2(hours) + 30. For 6 hours studying: predicted score = 5.2(6)+30 = 61.2.

lessons.tip: Always ask: is there a confounding variable? Two variables can be strongly correlated without one causing the other. Look for hidden third variables that might explain the relationship!

quiz.q: r = -0.9 indicates:
quiz.explanation: -0.9 is close to -1: strong negative linear relationship.

quiz.q: Correlation implies causation?
quiz.explanation: NEVER! Correlation does not imply causation. Always check for confounders.

quiz.q: r = 0.15 means:
quiz.explanation: r near 0 means very weak or no linear relationship.

quiz.q: A scatter plot shows points going down-left to up-right. Correlation is:
quiz.explanation: Upward trend from left to right = positive association, r > 0.
